title: Hierarchical Outlines: Connecting Questions Across Four Games

scenes.title: From a broad question to detailed conditions
lines: If we have plenty of ideas but cannot find the rule we need, how should we group the list?
We will separate features from adjustment values in Two Point Museum, compare the scope of branches through Manor Lords and Against the Storm, then examine containment and connections in Timberborn.
Together, we will build a hierarchical outline that moves from the overall goal down to detailed conditions and back to the whole. Let us begin with an attraction being adjusted.

scenes.title: Village operations and individual choices
lines: Can we find questions of comparable scale in another game? In Manor Lords, players place village buildings and assign people to work. This is a development demonstration from 2022.
At the carpenter camp marked in red, the occupied assignment slots increase from one to two. Beneath the broad question of operating the workplace sits the more detailed question of who to assign.

In a separate market shot, Hide is chosen as the selling item and one worker is assigned to an empty slot. Selecting the product and assigning people are different conditions within market operations.

Our notes put workplace operations and market operations beside one another, with each choice beneath its own feature. This is a structure we create from observation, not a reconstruction of the developer's design document.

Continuously changing a ride's shape differs from selecting village options, but both let us distinguish a broad feature from its smaller conditions. Let us return to the museum and check whether the main flow remains readable when the details are folded.

scenes.title: Keep conditions under the appropriate branch
lines: We can check a branch's meaning against actual features. Against the Storm is a settlement game where resources are used to build structures and residents are assigned work. We are viewing a developer demonstration from 2024.

Rotating and placing the shelter marked in red first creates a foundation. In the later construction excerpt, one shelter has a finished roof while work beside it remains incomplete. Placement and completion must be distinguished.

Placing the mine's foundation opens construction requirements and production entries. A small fishing hut in another shot has bait settings. The mine's conditions and the fishing hut's conditions cannot be written as one identical rule.

In our outline, housing and resource production are sibling features, with each building's conditions under its appropriate branch. For a mine or hut still under construction, verifying the result remains an open question.

Move and reread those conditions together with their heading. We have now organized what belongs inside a feature. Let us continue to the track and entrance examples to examine how to record relationships that require checking another feature.

scenes.title: Ownership of settings and signal connections
lines: Can Timberborn show the difference between containment and references? Players build a beaver settlement and manage water. In this version 1.0 demonstration, a floodgate adjusts the height at which it blocks water, while a lever sends a manual signal.
The floodgate marked in red shows one meter for the signal's Off state and two meters for On. Its signal field selects the name Badtide. These are values displayed by the source interface.

Separately, switching the lever on changes its indicator from Off to On. We have observed a signal selection and a state change. We do not attach later footage of another map or waterway as proof that this operation succeeded.

Our notes place both heights and the signal choice under floodgate settings, with sending the lever's signal as a separate feature. A teal arrow points to the signal being referenced; it does not make the lever the document's parent.

Museum tracks, village assignments, settlement construction conditions, and floodgate connections involve different actions. The shared test is to distinguish where a condition belongs from its references to other features. Let us now return from the details to reviewing the overall goal.
